summary: Describes how to carry location information about a user's access network, in civic or geospatial formats, inside RADIUS and Diameter messages. Because location data is sensitive, the document also discusses privacy concerns around distributing it.

plainLanguage.summary: When you connect to a network, the network can tell the service where you are. This explains how to pass that note along, and why it needs careful handling because it is private.

questions: how does radius request location from a nas
subtitle: New RADIUS and Diameter attributes that let a network tell an authentication server where a user is, with privacy rules attached.

tldr.problem: A user's home network sometimes needs to know where the user is, for billing or authorization, but location is sensitive and RADIUS had no way to carry it.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new attributes carry the operator name, location metadata, civic or geospatial location data, policy rules and the capability and request flags, in several message flows.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8559, that makes policy rules travel with every location and requires message integrity protection.

today: RFC 5580 is a Proposed Standard. It is updated by RFC 8559 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Carry Location in RADIUS
sections.content:
RFC 5580 defines attributes for RADIUS and Diameter that convey location-related information inside authentication and accounting exchanges. Wireless networks in airports, hotels and coffee shops are run by many kinds of operators, and a home network may want the user's location for location-aware billing, authorization or other services.

Because location must be protected from unauthorized access and distribution, the design follows the GEOPRIV model of RFC 3693: a Location Generator, a Location Server, a Location Recipient and a Rule Maker. Appendix A compares the GEOPRIV requirements with what this document provides.

To the RADIUS server the location parts are opaque data. A location-server component used alongside the RADIUS server processes and distributes them, with access control and privacy protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes your home service wants to know where you connected from, like a shop that wants to know which branch you visited. But where you are is private, so the note adds rules for who may see it.

sections.title: Four Ways to Deliver Location
sections.content:
The RFC describes four delivery methods. In the first, an out-of-band agreement between the RADIUS client (the Network Access Server, or NAS) and the server lets the NAS attach location attributes to the Access-Request unprompted. This only suits cases such as client and server in the same administrative domain.

In the second, the NAS includes a Location-Capable attribute. If the server needs location and did not get it, it may send an Access-Challenge with a Requested-Location-Info hint, and the NAS answers in a new Access-Request. The NAS treats the policy rule attributes as opaque and echoes them back.

In the third, mid-session delivery uses the Change-of-Authorization messages of RFC 5176. The server must return Requested-Location-Info with the FUTURE_REQUESTS flag in the Access-Accept; later a CoA-Request with Service-Type Authorize Only makes the NAS send an Access-Request with the location. The fourth reports location in accounting messages, for example when different tariffs or tax rates apply by location.
sections.plainLanguage: The shop can get your location in four ways: you tell it as you walk in, it asks you and you answer, it calls you later and asks again, or it reads it off the receipt at the end.

sections.title: The Seven Attributes
sections.content:
Operator-Name (126) holds a namespace ID and the name of the access network owner, at most 253 bytes. The four namespaces are TADIG, REALM, E212 and ICC, written as the ASCII characters 0 to 3.

Location-Information (127) carries metadata: an Index, a Code (0 for civic, 1 for geospatial), an Entity (0 for the user's client device, 1 for the RADIUS client), a Sighting Time, a Time-to-Live and a Method. Location-Data (128) carries the location itself, linked by the Index. The civic profile follows the encoding of RFC 4776 and the geospatial profile follows the format of RFC 3825, in both cases without the leading DHCP option code and length.

Basic-Location-Policy-Rules (129) holds a retransmission-allowed flag, a Retention Expires time and a Note Well URI. Extended-Location-Policy-Rules (130) holds only a URI, preferably HTTPS, to a richer rule set. Location-Capable (131) and Requested-Location-Info (132) are bit maps, with values such as CIVIC_LOCATION (1), GEO_LOCATION (2), USERS_LOCATION (4) and NAS_LOCATION (8). The request also has FUTURE_REQUESTS (16) and NONE (32).
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute is a labelled slot in the message: one for who runs the network, one for where, one for how sure we are, and others for the privacy rules and for asking and answering.

sections.title: Use in Diameter
sections.content:
In Diameter the attributes are used as attribute-value pairs from the code space 1-255, the RADIUS attribute-compatibility space, so no new Diameter codes are allocated. All seven are of type OctetString. A gateway between RADIUS and Diameter copies them as they are, apart from changes to headers, alignment and padding.

What the RFC says about an Access-Request applies in Diameter to the AA-Request or Diameter-EAP-Request, and what it says about a CoA-Request applies to the Re-Auth-Request. Accounting-Request carries over as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter is a newer cousin of RADIUS, so the same labelled slots work there too, with almost no changes.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Without authentication, integrity and replay protection between RADIUS entities, an adversary could spoof or alter the attributes. RADIUS over IPsec is the preferred protection, and confidentiality protection MUST be used to stop eavesdroppers reading location. Where IPsec is not available, an Access-Request carrying location attributes without a Message-Authenticator SHOULD be silently discarded by the server, and a server or NAS that supports the attributes MUST silently discard a packet whose Message-Authenticator does not match.

On privacy, the client discloses location only under an out-of-band agreement or when the server asks. A RADIUS client MUST pass location to other entities only together with the policy rules, and the receiver MUST follow them. The server MUST attach the privacy rules whenever it makes location available to others. A proxy must follow both sets of rules.

The RFC also warns that identity and location are tightly coupled. A fixed MAC address, identity revealed during EAP or CHAP, static data in the Class attribute, or long-term identifiers from mobility or application protocols can let a visited network or broker correlate location with a particular user and learn their movement patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Location is like a diary of where you have been. The note says to lock the envelope in transit and to staple the privacy rules to every copy, and it warns that your name on the envelope can give you away.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA registered the seven attributes in the RADIUS namespaces and in the Diameter namespace, and allocated the value 509 in the Error-Cause registry for Location-Info-Required. A server can answer an Access-Challenge that went unanswered with an Access-Reject carrying that error.

New registries cover operator namespace identifiers (new values from 0x34 to 0xFE by Expert Review), location profiles, the Location-Capable bit map (32 bits, 4 defined), entity types, privacy flags and the Requested-Location-Info bit map.
sections.plainLanguage: The note also asks the official keeper of number lists to write the new labels down, so everyone uses the same numbers.
